query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy nanoalloys, rapid synthesis by laser‐induced thermionic emission reduction kinetically traps a homogeneous, metastable atomic configuration that suppresses diffusion‐driven phase segregation at high temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogeneous, equimolar high-entropy nanoalloy nanoparticles (e.g., PtPdCoCuNi) produced via a fast, laser-induced reduction process on a defective carbon support.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of nanoalloy samples: one synthesized via rapid laser-induced thermionic emission reduction and one via a conventional, slower chemical reduction method.
generation.conditions: Expose each set to an elevated temperature range (e.g., 600–900 K) under an inert atmosphere to minimize oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale particle size (1–3 nm) and the defective carbon interfacing from the laser process that limits atom mobility.
generation.mechanism: Fast synthesis locks in a metastable, well-mixed phase by outrunning atomic diffusion mechanisms that drive phase segregation. In contrast, slower synthesis allows elemental diffusional rearrangement that promotes chemical inhomogeneity at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: After high-temperature exposure, nanoalloys synthesized by the rapid laser method will maintain a single, homogeneous phase with minimal segregation, whereas conventionally synthesized nanoalloys will show detectable phase separation and chemical inhomogeneity.
generation.baseline: Conventionally synthesized high-entropy nanoalloys (with the same overall composition) prepared by slower reduction methods.
generation.boundary: This prediction applies to nanoalloys on carbon supports with particle sizes of approximately 1–3 nm and for temperature ranges where atomic diffusion becomes significant but not dominant (up to about 900 K), particularly for systems containing immiscible elements.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature threshold at which diffusion overrides kinetic trapping, and the influence of slight variations in alloy composition and support interactions, remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of identically composed HENA nanoparticles: one via rapid laser-induced thermionic emission reduction and one via a conventional slow synthesis method. Subject both sets to high-temperature annealing (600–900 K) in an inert atmosphere. After treatment, evaluate the phase purity, chemical homogeneity, and microstructure using X-ray diffraction (XRD), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS).
measurements: XRD peak analysis for phase segregation or splitting
TEM imaging for particle morphology and size changes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both synthesis methods yield nanoalloys with similar levels of homogeneity and phase stability after high-temperature treatment, or if the rapid synthesis samples show no significant improvement over the conventional samples, then the hypothesis that kinetic trapping governs high-temperature stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Nanoalloys, especially high-entropy nanoalloys (HENAs) that contain equal stoichiometric metallic elements in each nanoparticle, are widely used in vast applications. Currently, the synthesis of HENAs is challenged by slow reaction kinetics that leads to phase segregation, sophisticated pretreatment of precursors, and inert conditions that preclude scalable fabrication of HENAs. Here, we report direct conversion of metal salts to ultrafine HENAs on carbonaceous support by nanosecond pulsed laser under atmospheric conditions. Because of the unique laser-induced thermionic emission and etch on carbon, the reduced metal elements were gathered to ultrafine HENAs and stabilized by defective carbon support. This scalable, facile, and low-cost method overcomes the immiscible issue and can produce various HENAs uniformly with a size of 1 to 3 nanometers and metal elements up to 11 with productivity up to 7 grams per hour. One of the senary HENAs exhibited excellent catalytic performance in oxygen reduction reaction, manifesting great potential in practical applications. Scalable fabriction of ultrasmall high-entropy nanoalloys is realized by laser-induced thermionic emission reduction.

Metal nanoalloys are critical catalysts and widely used in many chemical reactions ranging from environmental to energy fields (). Conventional bottom-up routes, such as wet-chemistry methods for the synthesis of metal nanoalloys, usually need to consider the miscibility of each metallic element in the phase diagrams to avoid the phase segregation during the formation of the particles (). The immiscible issue of metals restricts the realm of nanoalloys and precludes the discovery of new nanoalloys with superior functionalities (). In recent years, high-entropy nanoalloys (HENAs) containing equal stoichiometric ratios of various metals in each particle in a well-mixed manner have attracted a lot of interest because of their unusual physical and chemical properties. These unique properties make them attractive as catalysts (), such as oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) that has great potential for applications in energy and environmental science. Recent studies have revealed that the slow reaction kinetics in traditional methods is one of the major obstacles that lead to the phase segregation in nanoalloys (, ).
